clue.text: Devoured one sheep, noisily

indicators.note: something done noisily is heard rather than seen, so we go by sound not spelling

blocks.note: one is A, and a tup is a ram, a male sheep

explanation.surface: Someone wolfed down an entire sheep, and loudly at that.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'a tup' runs together as ATE UP. TUP is a dialect and farming word for a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat something up is to consume all of it greedily, the phrasal verb for finishing food completely.

clue.text: Growth in understanding

blocks.note: first meaning: a rise in value, as of property or shares
second meaning: grasp or recognition of something's worth

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one idea, growing in understanding; split it at 'in' and each side is a separate sense of the same noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Assets gain value through rising prices, and a person shows insight by grasping a situation; the noun covers both senses.

clue.text: Worthy folks incense me terribly

indicators.note: something done terribly is botched, so these letters come out in a mangled order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Pompous dignitaries make the speaker absolutely furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incense' looks like the verb to anger, but it is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Eminence is a title of honour for cardinals and, more loosely, distinguished or important people generally.

clue.text: In France, slight appetite, taking only part

indicators.note: taking only part of something means a section is lifted out of a longer word

blocks.note: the run of letters inside the word, after AP and before E

explanation.surface: A diner in France has little appetite and eats only a portion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' flags that the answer is a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Petit is the French adjective for small or minor, matching slight in a French setting.

clue.text: You shouldn’t have small infatuation in Australian state

blocks.note: what you say on receiving a gift; TA is British informal thanks
S is the abbreviation for small
a mania is a craze or obsession

explanation.surface: A gentle rebuke to someone harbouring a small crush while visiting Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You shouldn't have' sounds like disapproval but is the polite phrase on getting a present, i.e. thanks, and TA is British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasmania is the island state lying south of the Australian mainland, an example of the category.

clue.text: Where to cook morsel for Tolkien’s hero

definitions.note: the book title stands for its hobbit hero

blocks.note: the hob is the cooking surface on top of a stove
a bit is a small piece

explanation.surface: A question of where to prepare a snack for Bilbo Baggins.
explanation.walkthrough: HOB is the British word for a cooker's top burners, and the article comes along with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bilbo Baggins, the central character of Tolkien's first novel, belongs to the small hairy-footed race the title names.

clue.text: Either side in scrimmage might be hurt

indicators.note: a side of a word is one of its edges, so only an end letter is used

blocks.note: the first letter, the left-hand edge of the word
either pairs with OR to offer alternatives
the last letter, the right-hand edge of the word

explanation.surface: In a rugby scrum, players on both sides could end up injured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Either side' is read literally: the side letter is S or E, written out as S-OR-E.
explanation.definitionFit: A sore limb is painful or injured, so the adjective matches being hurt.

clue.text: A little bean tip as topping in canapé

indicators.note: a little of a phrase is just a portion of it, lifted out of the surrounding words

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning these words, after BE and before PPING

explanation.surface: A tiny dab of bean as the garnish on a party nibble.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden run starts inside 'bean' and ends inside 'topping'.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasto is an Italian starter of small savoury bites, broadly comparable to an appetiser or party snack.

clue.text: Opening part of chain letter

indicators.note: part of a phrase is a section of it, so the letters sit inside the words

blocks.note: the run after CHA and before TER

explanation.surface: The first paragraph of a chain letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' looks like the start of the letter, but it is the definition, as a noun meaning a gap.
explanation.definitionFit: An inlet is a narrow way in, of water into land or air into an engine, so a kind of gap or entry.

clue.text: Tipsy tippler, tattler giving you stuff and nonsense

indicators.note: a tipsy person staggers about unsteadily, so these letters lurch into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drunk drinker and a gossip pour out a stream of rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tipsy' seems to describe the tippler, but it governs both words that follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: This rhyming reduplication means trivial, empty chatter, matching rubbish talk; it is an old variant of prattle.

clue.text: Short fellow inserting limb in long johns?

definitions.note: an example, hence the question mark

indicators.note: inserting puts one thing inside another, so one piece goes into the middle of the next

blocks.note: under, as in coming in under the mark, means falling short
a gent is a man
an arm is a limb

explanation.surface: A little man trying to get his leg into his thermal leggings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short fellow' looks like one idea, a small man, but it splits into two pieces. The limb could be LEG, but only ARM fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Long johns are full-length underpants worn for warmth, one example of clothing worn beneath outer layers.

clue.text: Sporting Coe let in: it's how parliamentarians are chosen

indicators.note: sporting can mean playing about, so these letters are played with

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The athlete Sebastian Coe was admitted to the Lords through sporting fame, and that is how members get there.
explanation.walkthrough: Sebastian Coe, the Olympic runner turned politician, gives the surface its sporting angle; his name is only letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a parliament are picked by voters at a poll, which is what this word names.

clue.text: Exactly zero t-shirts etc. returned

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: no as in none, nil
t-shirts are examples of tops

explanation.surface: Precisely no shirts came back from the laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exactly zero' reads as one phrase, but 'Exactly' is the definition. SPOT-ON is British informal for precisely right.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot-on is British slang for completely accurate, so it fits as an adverb or adjective meaning precisely.

clue.text: Translation of banal epic not up to the job

indicators.note: a translation renders words in another form, so these letters are recast

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dull rendering of a heroic poem that fails to do it justice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translation' looks literary, fitting the epic, but it only asks for the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lacking the ability or competence for a task is unable to do it, which this adjective says.

clue.text: Not starting rhinoscopic process, finally wanting changes for one with ‘incredible’ nasal abnormality

indicators.note: something not starting has lost its beginning, so the opening letter goes
finally points at the end, so only the closing letter is taken
wanting means lacking, so that letter is removed
changes means alters, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word without its first letter
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A medical description of a nose examination for someone with an unbelievable nasal condition.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the R, then drop the S of 'process' from what remains and rearrange. Rhinoscopy is examining the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: The puppet's nose grows whenever he lies, so his deformity is linked to telling things that are not credible.

clue.text: Former husband rapped and sermonized

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
to rap is to knock or strike

explanation.surface: An ex-husband knocked on the door and then lectured everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' sits inside the definition's verb pair in the surface but is really only joining the wordplay to it.
explanation.definitionFit: To expound is to set out and explain at length, as a preacher does from the pulpit.

clue.text: With coins of little value, Everyman’s heading to find boozer

indicators.note: the heading of something is its top, so only the opening letter is used

blocks.note: a sou was a small French coin, proverbially worthless
the opening letter of the setter's name

explanation.surface: The setter, carrying only small change, goes off looking for a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub, which suits the surface, but here it means a heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: A souse is a drunkard, someone habitually soaked in alcohol, so it names a heavy drinker.

clue.text: Far from welcome seeing football team gathering in vain: not half

indicators.note: to gather is to collect in, so one piece takes another inside it
not half means only half survives, so the back half of the letters is cut

blocks.note: United is a common football club name, such as Manchester United
the first three of its six letters

explanation.surface: A disliked side gathers in a doomed attempt, and not half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' is British slang for 'very much', but here it literally halves the preceding phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A guest nobody asked to come is not wanted at the event, which is the opposite of being welcome.

clue.text: Heavyweight’s disheartened, Sonny Liston’s fourth struggle

indicators.note: losing heart means losing the centre, so the middle letter goes
fourth picks out the letter in that position in the word
a struggle is a tussle, so the letters wrestle into a new order

blocks.note: the word without its middle letter
the letter in fourth place

explanation.surface: A dejected boxer is in his fourth fight against Sonny Liston.
explanation.walkthrough: Sonny Liston was a world heavyweight boxing champion of the 1960s, so the surface stays in the ring; his name supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Mike Tyson was undisputed world champion in boxing's top weight division, an example of such a fighter.

clue.text: Cuckoo, pigeon and tit moving stealthily

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so these letters go haywire

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Three birds creep quietly along together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuckoo' poses as a third bird in the list, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking on the balls of the feet keeps footsteps quiet, so it is creeping about without being heard.

clue.text: Aim to express disapproval

blocks.note: first meaning: a goal or purpose, as a noun
second meaning: to protest, as a verb

explanation.walkthrough: 'Aim to' reads like a verb with an infinitive; in fact 'Aim' is a noun and 'to' just links the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the word means a purpose or goal; as a verb, stressed on the second syllable, it means to protest.

clue.text: Mutual club?

blocks.note: first meaning: shared, held in common
second meaning: a nightclub or bar, in slang

explanation.walkthrough: The pair looks like a society for members, but the two words are separate senses; the question mark flags the slang one.
explanation.definitionFit: A shared account is held in common, and informally a seedy bar or nightspot is called by the same word.

clue.text: Money changing hands for pudding

blocks.note: first meaning: the total sales a business takes
second meaning: a folded pastry with fruit inside, such as an apple one

explanation.surface: Someone paying cash for a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pudding' is the British word for dessert generally.
explanation.definitionFit: A business's volume of sales is its takings, and a pastry folded over a filling is a classic baked dessert.

clue.text: Natal’s yammering animal – large antelope, primarily?

definitions.text: Natal’s yammering animal – large antelope, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is used

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of these five words

explanation.surface: A noisy creature from Natal, a big antelope at first glance.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a description: Natal is a province of South Africa, home to this antelope.
explanation.definitionFit: The nyala is a spiral-horned southern African antelope, found in KwaZulu-Natal, so the clue describes it.

clue.text: Issue a reproach when fibber's shown up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a fibber tells lies

explanation.surface: Telling someone off once a liar is exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shown up' looks like exposed, but in a down clue it turns the word upward.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail against something is to complain bitterly or scold, which is voicing a reproach.

clue.text: At length, a child trained hairy bovines

indicators.note: trained means shaped or drilled into form, so these letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: After much effort, a youngster schooled some shaggy cows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At length' looks like scene-setting, but every letter is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: This Scottish breed of cow has long shaggy coats and long horns, so they are shaggy-haired cows.

clue.text: Son caused online trouble, proceeded without urgency

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
to troll is to provoke people on the internet

explanation.surface: A boy stirred up an internet row and then took his time about it.
explanation.walkthrough: To troll is to post provocative messages online to upset people, a modern sense the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: To walk at a leisurely pace is to amble along, moving forward in no hurry.

clue.text: Gold, Dutch and Italian, in financial examination

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
D is the abbreviation for Dutch
IT is the abbreviation for Italian

explanation.surface: Gold held by Dutch and Italian investors comes under scrutiny from the accountants.
explanation.walkthrough: AU comes from the Latin aurum; D and IT are standard abbreviations for the nationalities.
explanation.definitionFit: An official inspection of an organisation's accounts by an independent checker is this kind of review.
